title: Finding the nearest car
teaches: Cells and space-filling curves (geohash, quadtrees, S2, H3), a stream of location updates held in memory, and sharding by cell

blocks.text: In 2015 Matt Ranney, then chief systems architect at Uber, gave a talk on how its dispatch system worked. Every driver's phone running the app sent its position to Uber's servers every few seconds, about every four, whether or not the driver had a passenger. A rider opening the app expected to see the cars near them moving on the map within a second, and a request for a ride had to find a free car close by and offer it the trip. Behind both was one question asked thousands of times a second: which of the cars moving about this city are near this point now?

A database answers "find the row with this key" quickly because its index is sorted, and nearness in one dimension is nearness in the sorted order. A position has two dimensions, latitude and longitude, and no single sort order keeps every pair of nearby points together. This lesson is about the tricks that come close: cutting the map into cells and numbering them so that nearby cells mostly get nearby numbers, which turns "what is near here?" into a few lookups in an ordinary sorted or hashed store. Lesson M1's tiles already cut the map into cells, named by zoom, column and row; what they lack is a single number in which nearby tiles get nearby values.

Start with the load. Suppose a million drivers online at the busiest hour, each sending a position every four seconds: 250,000 updates a second. An update is a driver's ID, a latitude, a longitude, a time and a state (free, offered a trip, carrying a passenger), about 50 bytes, so 12.5 MB a second comes in. Each update replaces the last one from the same driver, and a position is useless after half a minute. The whole live picture is a million records of 50 bytes, 50 MB: it fits in the memory of one ordinary server many times over. Reads are fewer but each is a search; say 100,000 searches a second at the peak.

The first design that comes to mind is a table of drivers in a relational database, with an index on latitude and one on longitude, and a query for rows whose latitude and longitude both fall within a small box around the rider. It fails twice. An index on latitude narrows the search only to a band around the whole planet: the latitudes of Manhattan run on through Spain, Italy, Turkey and northern China, and every driver along that band stays in the running until the longitude check throws them out. And each of the 250,000 updates a second rewrites two index entries on disk and in a log, for data that will be thrown away four seconds later. Positions belong in memory, with a copy appended to a log such as lesson 16's Kafka for anyone who needs the history later.

In 2008 Gustavo Niemeyer published **geohash**, which turns a position into a short string.[^geohash] It halves the range of longitude and writes a 1 if the point is in the east half and a 0 if in the west, then does the same for latitude, and so on, alternating, each bit halving the cell. The bits are written five at a time as characters of a 32-letter alphabet. Every extra character divides the cell's area by 32: five characters name a cell about 5 km on a side, six about 1.2 km by 0.6 km, seven about 150 m. Points in the same cell share a prefix, so a store sorted by geohash keeps each cell's drivers together, and a cell's drivers are one range scan.

Two problems follow. The first is edges. Two cars a metre apart on either side of a cell boundary are in different cells, and at the biggest boundaries, the equator or the prime meridian, their geohashes share not even a first character. So a search never scans only the rider's cell: it scans every cell its circle touches, which for a circle smaller than a cell means the rider's cell and up to eight around it. The second is that one cell size does not fit a whole country. A cell that holds three drivers in Montana holds three hundred in Manhattan at six in the evening.

A **quadtree** (Raphael Finkel and Jon Bentley, 1974) adapts to density: start with one square, and whenever a square holds more than some number of points, split it into four. Cities end up cut fine and countryside coarse, so every cell holds about the same number. **Hexagons** answer a different problem: the centres of a square's four edge neighbours are one cell width from its own centre and those of its four corner neighbours about 1.41 widths, while all six of a hexagon's neighbours have centres the same distance away, which makes hexagons better for spreading a count of riders or drivers smoothly over an area.

blocks.caption: 400 drivers on a 20 km square, most of them in a city centre, and a search for those within 1.5 km of the blue point. Shaded cells are the ones the search must scan. Tap the map to move the search.
blocks.task: Try each way of cutting the map

blocks.text: In the city centre a fixed grid of 2.5 km squares makes a search scan a few hundred drivers to find the few dozen within a kilometre and a half; the quadtree's small city cells scan far fewer. Move the search into the country and the grid and the quadtree both scan nearly empty cells. The quadtree's price is that its cells change as drivers move, so the tree must be kept up to date or rebuilt every few seconds.

Geohash numbers its cells along a **Z-order curve**: interleaving the bits visits the four quarters of a square in the order of the letter Z, then each quarter's quarters the same way. Cells next to each other in the numbering are usually next to each other on the map, but the curve makes long jumps, from the end of one Z to the start of the next, and cells side by side across a jump get numbers far apart.

Google's **S2** library, written by Eric Veach, numbers cells along a **Hilbert curve** instead, a path that visits every cell of a grid while always stepping to a neighbour, so consecutive numbers are always adjacent cells.[^hilbert] S2 puts the Earth inside a cube, projects each of the cube's six faces onto the sphere, and cuts each face as a quadtree up to 30 levels deep, where a cell is about a centimetre across. A cell's 64-bit ID is its face and its path down the tree, in Hilbert order. Any region, a circle round a rider or the outline of a city, becomes a **covering**: a handful of cells of mixed sizes, and so a handful of ranges of IDs.

blocks.caption: An 8 by 8 grid numbered along a Z-order curve and along a Hilbert curve, and a search over 9 cells. Each run of consecutive numbers is one range scan in a store sorted by cell number.
blocks.task: Switch to the Hilbert curve and move the search about

blocks.text: This is what makes cells useful to the stores of earlier lessons. Bigtable (lesson 10) keeps rows sorted by key, so a table keyed by S2 cell ID, with the item's own ID after it, answers "everything in this region" with a few range scans. A hashed store such as lesson 12's Dynamo cannot scan ranges, but it can hold one entry per cell listing what is in it, and a search reads the few cells of its covering by key.

Uber released its own grid, **H3**, in 2018. It covers the Earth with hexagons at 16 resolutions, from cells with edges about 1,100 km long down to edges under a metre, each cell holding about seven of the next size down.[^pentagons] Uber uses it to count supply and demand across a city, to set prices by area and to forecast, the jobs where equal distance to every neighbour matters. For finding the nearest car, squares in a sorted store are simpler; for counting across a city, hexagons are smoother.

The live index is two maps in memory. One maps each driver's ID to its latest record: cell, position, time and state. The other maps each cell to the set of drivers in it. An update looks up the driver; if the cell has changed, it moves the driver from one set to the other; then it overwrites the record. A driver not heard from for thirty seconds is dropped. A search computes the cells its circle touches, reads their sets, checks each driver's true distance and state, and ranks the free ones by estimated time to reach the rider, which lesson M3 shows how to compute. The cell size is chosen per search: S2 picks the level whose cells are about the size of the circle, so a covering is at most eight or so cells. A search for the k nearest free cars has no radius to start with. It reads the rider's cells; if it finds fewer than k, or the k-th is farther away than the edge of the area read, a nearer car could lie just outside, so it widens the ring of cells and reads again.

One server could hold all of it, but not answer 250,000 updates and 100,000 searches a second with room to spare, nor survive its own failure. So the index is split by cell across many servers, each owning the cells that consistent hashing (lessons 5 and 12) gives it. Uber built a library for this, Ringpop: the servers find each other and agree on who is alive by gossip, place themselves on a hash ring, and any server receiving a request for a cell forwards it to the cell's owner.[^swim] A search whose circle crosses cells on two or three servers asks each of them, a small fan-out. Lesson 9 showed that a fanned-out request waits for the slowest server it asks, which costs little at two or three.

Splitting by cell has the same weakness as lesson 10's row keys that start with a timestamp: load follows the cells, and the cells are not equal. A city centre at rush hour sends most updates to the few servers that own its cells.

blocks.caption: Position updates hashed by cell to four shards, in slow motion. With one cell size, the city centre is a few busy cells; with cells cut smaller where drivers are dense, its load spreads over many.
blocks.task: Raise the updates to 400 a second or more, then cut busy cells smaller

blocks.text: To grow the design by ten times, 2.5 million updates a second: at 100,000 updates a second for a server working in memory, that is 25 shards, and a search still touches only the two or three servers its cells live on. At a hundred times, 250 shards, and a search still touches two or three. What grows badly is a hot city, and the fix is the quadtree's idea applied to the shards: cut the busy cells finer, at a deeper S2 level, so a busy centre spreads over many owners, and leave the countryside in large cells.

The nearest free car is not always the right one to send. Suppose rider A asks first. Driver X is 2 minutes from A and driver Y is 3 minutes away. A moment later rider B asks, and B is 2 minutes from X but 10 minutes from Y. Sending each rider the nearest free car as they ask gives A the car X and leaves B with Y: 2 + 10 = 12 minutes of driving to pick both up. Waiting a couple of seconds, collecting both requests, and matching them together gives A the car Y and B the car X: 3 + 2 = 5 minutes. Batching trades a short wait for every rider against much less driving across the city, and the matching becomes an assignment problem solved over each batch.

Then the offer. The chosen driver is offered the trip and has a few seconds to accept; if not, the next driver in line is offered it. A driver must never be offered two trips at once, which is a lesson 11 problem in miniature: the driver's state changes from free to offered only if it is still free, a compare-and-set on the one server that owns that driver's record, so two searches that both found the same free driver cannot both win.

blocks.title: The shape of the design
points: Positions are overwritten every few seconds: keep them in memory, and log a copy.
Cells turn two dimensions into keys; search every cell the circle touches, not just one.
A Hilbert-ordered cell ID makes a region a few range scans in a sorted store.
Shard by cell, and cut cells finer where drivers are dense.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on finding what is nearby
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Two cars are a metre apart, but their geohashes share no prefix at all. What explains it?
choices: Geohash rounds positions to the nearest kilometre, so close points can land anywhere
One of the cars sent its position in degrees and the other in radians
They sit either side of a major cell boundary, such as the equator
items.why: Points in the same cell share a prefix, but nearby points across a boundary can be in cells whose names differ from the first character. That is why a search covers every cell its circle touches.

items.ask: A million drivers each send a position every 4 seconds. How many updates a second must the system take, and where should the latest positions live?
choices: 250,000 a second, in memory, with a copy appended to a log
4 million a second, on disk in an indexed table
25,000 a second, in a relational table with indexes on latitude and longitude
items.why: 1,000,000 ÷ 4 = 250,000. Each update overwrites the last and is stale within seconds, so memory suits it; the history goes to a log for later use.

items.ask: Why does a table indexed on latitude answer "drivers within 2 km of this point" poorly?
choices: Latitude cannot be stored in an index, because it is a floating-point number
The latitude index narrows the search only to a band around the whole planet
An index on latitude sorts drivers by distance from the equator, not from the rider
items.why: A thin range of latitudes still crosses every longitude, so the query reads every driver in every city in that band before the longitude test discards them.

items.ask: Why is a quadtree a better fit than a fixed grid for drivers spread over a country?
choices: It needs no updating as drivers move, because its cells never change
It gives every cell six neighbours at equal distances, which a grid cannot
It splits cells where drivers are dense, so each cell holds about the same number
items.why: A fixed grid's city cells overflow while its rural cells sit empty. The quadtree adapts its cell size to density, at the cost of keeping the tree current as drivers move.

items.ask: What does numbering cells along a Hilbert curve give a store sorted by cell ID?
choices: Every cell's ID is shorter, so the store holds more cells in the same memory and scans faster
Consecutive IDs are always neighbouring cells, so a two-dimensional region becomes a few range scans
Each cell's four neighbours have IDs one apart, so any circular search is a single range scan
items.why: The Hilbert curve never jumps, so nearby cells mostly fall in a few runs of consecutive IDs. It cannot make every neighbour consecutive in two dimensions, so a search still needs several ranges.

items.ask: Driver positions are sharded by cell. At rush hour the one server that owns the city centre's few cells is overloaded while the others idle. What is the best fix?
choices: Cut the busy cells finer, so the city centre's load spreads over more owners
Add more servers to the ring, keeping every cell at the size it is now
Send each update to every server, so any of them can answer any search
items.why: Each hot cell is owned by one server however many servers the ring has, so adding servers leaves the hot cells where they are. Finer cells where drivers are dense turn a few hot keys into many, which hashing then spreads.

items.ask: Two riders and two drivers: A is 2 minutes from X and 3 from Y; B is 2 minutes from X and 10 from Y. A asks first. Which matching is better, and how is it found?
choices: A gets X and B gets Y, 12 minutes in all, found by giving each rider the nearest free car
A gets X and B waits for X to finish, found by queueing riders for the nearest car
A gets Y and B gets X, 5 minutes in all, found by matching a short batch of requests together
items.why: Greedy matching gives A the nearest car and strands B 10 minutes away. Batching a couple of seconds of requests and solving the assignment together cuts total pickup time from 12 minutes to 5.

summary: **Do the arithmetic before choosing a store.** A million drivers every four seconds is 250,000 updates a second of data that is stale within seconds, so it lives in memory with a copy logged.
**An index on latitude and longitude is the wrong tool.** A latitude range is a band round the planet, and the updates would rewrite the indexes constantly.
**Cells turn a position into a key.** Geohash interleaves the bits of latitude and longitude, so points in one cell share a prefix.
**Search every cell the circle touches.** Nearby points across a boundary can have unrelated cell names.
**A quadtree fits cell size to density; hexagons give equal neighbours.** Fine cells in cities, coarse in the country; hexagons suit counting demand.
**S2 numbers cells along a Hilbert curve.** A region becomes a covering of a few cells and a few range scans in a sorted store.
**Shard by cell and split the hot cells.** Load follows cells, so busy centres are cut finer to spread over more servers.
**Matching a batch beats the nearest car.** Waiting a couple of seconds to assign several requests together can cut total pickup time a great deal.

geohash.title: A short link for a place
geohash.text: Niemeyer launched geohash as a public service at geohash.org, a short link for a location in the way TinyURL (lesson 3) gave short links for web pages: a position became a few characters you could paste anywhere. Its use as a database key came after.

hilbert.title: Hilbert's curve
hilbert.text: David Hilbert described the curve in 1891 as a curiosity: repeat its construction for ever and the path passes through every point of the square. Programs stop after a fixed number of levels, which gives a path through every cell of a grid that never jumps.

pentagons.title: Twelve pentagons
pentagons.text: A sphere cannot be covered with hexagons alone. H3 starts from an icosahedron, a solid of 20 triangles, and at every resolution there are exactly 12 pentagons, at its corners, placed in the oceans. A hexagon's seven children do not exactly fill it, so a cell's area is only roughly the sum of its children's.

swim.title: Gossip
swim.text: Ringpop's membership used SWIM (Abhinandan Das, Indranil Gupta and Ashish Motivala, 2002): each server pings a random other one now and then, asks others to try when a ping goes unanswered, and passes news of who has joined or died along with its pings, so word of a failure reaches every server in a few rounds without any central list.
